hero.name: Ramesh
hero.who: a 54-year-old hardware shop owner in Indore who lives in old regrets and new worries

story.b: Ramesh pulls up the shutter of his hardware shop in Indore at nine sharp. By nine fifteen his mind is somewhere else. Usually it is twelve years back, on the cement deal that cost him four lakh rupees. Sometimes it is ten years ahead, wondering if his son will ever care about the shop. A customer asks for brass hinges and Ramesh hands him the wrong size. His wife sends poha in a steel tiffin and he eats it frowning at the ledger, then cannot say how it tasted. One evening his daughter asks what he is always thinking about. Ramesh opens his mouth and finds no good answer. Nothing is actually wrong today, and still he goes to bed tired.

ask.q: Ramesh feels tired though nothing is wrong today. What is the most useful first step for him?
o: Plan a long holiday so he finally gets a break from the shop
Start noticing where his mind goes, instead of following every thought
Go over the cement deal once more until he makes peace with it
ask.why: A holiday moves his body, but his mind would carry the same replay along. Going over the old deal again is more of the same loop. Simply noticing his thoughts is the first step, because a man who can see the replay running is already a little outside it.

chapters.take: A busy mind cannot rest until you notice how busy it is.

story.b: On a slow afternoon, Ramesh sits at the counter and tries something new. He does not chase his thoughts. He just watches them, the way he watches trucks rumble past on the main road outside. There goes the cement deal again. There goes the worry about his son's marks. Here comes a complaint about the supplier who is always late. At first he gets pulled along by every one. Then, for a few seconds at a time, he notices a thought as it arrives, and something strange happens. He is the one watching, not the one being dragged. The old loss feels a little less like him and a little more like a truck passing by. He tries it again the next afternoon, and the next.

ask.q: A week later, a thought about the old deal grabs Ramesh and he stays angry for an hour. What should he do?
o: Force the thought out by thinking hard about something cheerful
Decide that watching his thoughts simply does not work for him
Notice the thought when it next arrives, and let it pass like traffic
ask.why: Getting pulled in sometimes is normal, because noticing is a skill that grows slowly. Forcing a cheerful thought is just another fight with his mind, and quitting after one bad hour wastes the practice. Each time he notices a thought arriving, he steps a little outside it again.

chapters.take: You can watch your thoughts, which means you are more than them.

story.b: Every morning for years, Ramesh has eaten breakfast while reading supplier rates on his phone. One Tuesday he puts the phone face down. He looks at the poha properly for the first time in months. Yellow, soft, with crunchy sev on top and the squeeze of lemon his wife always adds. He tastes the fennel. He hears the pressure cooker next door and the milkman's bell. It takes only ten minutes, and he feels oddly rested. Later, when the old carpenter who buys nails every Thursday comes in, Ramesh actually listens to him instead of nodding. The carpenter mentions a new building project nearby. On any other day, Ramesh would have missed it completely.

ask.q: Ramesh's friend says enjoying poha is silly when there are bills to plan. Which reply fits the idea best?
o: Planning has its time, but while eating he can simply eat
His friend is right, so he should plan the bills over breakfast
He should stop planning altogether and live only for small pleasures
ask.why: Life only happens in the moment he is actually in. Planning bills over poha means he gets neither a good plan nor a good breakfast. Dropping all planning goes too far. The idea is to give full attention to whatever is in front of him, then move to the next thing.

chapters.take: Give full attention to what is in front of you, and you stop missing your life.

story.b: One night Ramesh wakes at two and his mind starts running. What if a big chain store opens nearby? What if the shop shuts in ten years? What if his son never finds his way? By three he is sitting up, heart racing, solving problems that do not exist yet. The next morning he tries a different system. He keeps a notebook for clock time, twenty minutes after opening, to plan real things like calling his accountant and reordering pipes. Then he closes it. When the worry comes back that night, he asks himself one plain question. Is there a problem in this room, right now? The fan turns. His wife sleeps. He is fine. Slowly, he falls asleep.

ask.q: At two in the morning, Ramesh starts fearing his shop will close in ten years. What should he do?
o: Get up and work out a full ten-year plan right away
Ask if there is a problem this moment, and save planning for his morning slot
Take the fear as a warning and start looking for a buyer for the shop
ask.why: Planning belongs to clock time, at his desk with a notebook and a clear head. At two in the morning the ten-year fear lives only in his mind, and in that room nothing is wrong. Planning half asleep feeds the worry, and selling on a night fear is a huge decision made in mind time.

chapters.take: Use the clock to plan, then come back. Right now is usually okay.

story.b: At a family lunch, Ramesh's brother-in-law mentions, casually, that he has bought a second flat. Ramesh feels a hot rush climb up from his stomach. It is the old feeling, the one that says he is the man who lost four lakh and never recovered. In the past he would have made a sharp remark about loans, and the lunch would have ended in silence. This time he notices the heat. He notices his jaw tightening and the words lining up in his mouth. He does not fight the feeling and he does not feed it. He just watches it, the way he watches his thoughts at the counter. In a minute it softens. He passes the raita and asks about the flat.

ask.q: The old anger is rushing up at lunch. What should Ramesh do in that moment?
o: Pause and calmly notice the heat rising, without feeding or fighting it
Say the sharp thing now, so the anger does not build up inside
Push the feeling down hard and pretend everything is perfectly fine
ask.why: The rush is old pain waking up, far bigger than one comment about a flat. Snapping feeds it and spoils the lunch. Pushing it down hard is still a fight, and it often bursts out later. Watching it calmly lets it pass without it taking charge of him.

chapters.take: Old hurt loses its grip when you watch it instead of obeying it.

story.h: The truck stuck on the highway
story.b: A builder has ordered three hundred PVC pipes for Saturday morning. On Friday evening the supplier calls. His truck is stuck behind a breakdown on the highway near Dewas and will not reach until Sunday. The old Ramesh would have shouted down the phone, paced the shop and spent the night cursing. This time he puts the phone down and takes three slow breaths. The truck is stuck. Shouting will not move it an inch. Once he accepts that, his head clears. He checks his godown and finds a hundred and twenty pipes. He calls the builder, explains honestly, and offers those on Saturday and the rest on Sunday. The builder grumbles, then agrees.

ask.q: Next week, a power cut stops Ramesh's billing computer during the evening rush. What would accepting, then acting, look like?
o: Complain loudly about the electricity board until the power comes back
Accept it quietly and send all the waiting customers home
Accept the cut calmly, then write bills by hand in the old register
ask.why: Anger at the electricity board adds stress but no light. Sending everyone home confuses acceptance with giving up. Accepting what is true right now clears his head, and then he can pick the useful step, like the old paper register in the drawer.

chapters.take: Accept what is happening first, then do the one useful thing you can.

story.h: A quieter man at the counter
story.b: A few months later, the shop looks exactly the same. Same shelves of hinges and screws, same dusty calendar. Ramesh is the one who has changed. He still thinks about the cement deal sometimes, but it passes like a truck on the main road. He eats his poha without the phone and actually tastes it. When the two o'clock worries come, he asks if anything is wrong right now, and usually goes back to sleep. One evening his son says he wants to study design, not join the shop. Ramesh feels the old fear rise, watches it, and then listens properly. His daughter tells her mother that Papa laughs more these days. Ramesh pretends not to hear, and smiles.

chapters.take: Life happens now, and now is usually kinder than the mind says.
